answer: Each grade of tea passes through its own sieve, and the sorter gauges the mesh and writes the grade in the gauge book. A island grade sorted on another sieve fails the book: the mesh must match the sorter's own gauge at the pigment of the sieve, and a strange sieve sorts coarse and fine together. Buying a false gauge record costs a forger 15,800 in bribes to the sorter and fees to the factory, and the terrace entry in the book is checked at every packing, so tea whose grade was never gauged is sent back to the sorter.
